items.support: For integrable real X_n, S_n=sum_{k=1}^n X_k satisfies the centered strong law if (S_n-E S_n)/n tends to zero almost surely. For identically distributed integrable variables this is S_n/n -> E X_1.
items.proof_plan: Separate existence of each mean from the IID common-mean specialization.

items.support: Independent square-integrable real variables with sup_n Var(X_n)<infinity satisfy the centered strong law.
items.proof_plan: Use b_n=n and bound the variance series by C sum n^-2. Clause audit: use only the almost-sure conclusion. In the convergence-criterion supplier, steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove this without the L2-completeness step 1.2: the variance-tail bound gives P(sup_{j>=m}|S_j-S_m|>t)<=v_m/t^2; the decreasing Cauchy-oscillation events have probability tending to zero. Countably many rational tolerances give a measurable finite path limit; Kronecker then gives the asserted normalization. The unused L2 clause omits its published completeness supplier's countable-choice hypothesis; that clause is Phase-3 debt, not used here.

items.support: IID square-integrable real X_n satisfy S_n/n -> E X_1 almost surely.
items.proof_plan: Identical distributions give the same variance and expectation; use the bounded-variance law.

items.support: For nonnegative measurable X (possibly extended), sum_{n>=1} P(X>n) <= E X <= 1+sum_{n>=1} P(X>n). Hence integrability is equivalent to tail-sum finiteness.
items.proof_plan: Integrate the decreasing tail function on successive unit intervals; inequalities remain valid with infinity. Endpoint atoms are handled by strict tails.

items.support: For identically distributed real X_n with E|X_1|<infinity, Y_n=X_n 1_{|X_n|<=n} differs from X_n only finitely often almost surely; independence is unnecessary.
items.proof_plan: Sum P(|X_n|>n) using the common law and the tail lemma, then BC1. Finite changes of sums divided by n vanish.

items.support: For identically distributed integrable real X_n and Y_n=X_n 1_{|X_n|<=n}, sum Var(Y_n)/n^2 <= 2 E|X_1| < infinity; independence is unnecessary.
items.proof_plan: Var(Y_n)<=E Y_n^2. Interchange the nonnegative series and expectation by thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral applied to the increasing finite sums of the nonnegative measurable functions t²1_{t≤n}/n² (not the monotone-real-sequence theorem). Use lem-integer-part to define m=ceil(t)=-floor(-t), so m-1<t<=m. For t<=1, t^2 sum n^-2<=2t. For t>1, sum_{n>=m} n^-2<=1/m^2+1/m<=2/t. Integrate t^2 sum_{n>=max(1,ceil(t))} n^-2 against the law of |X_1|. This includes integer endpoints correctly.

items.support: With the same identically distributed integrable variables, n^-1 sum_{k<=n} E[X_k 1_{|X_k|<=k}] -> E X_1.
items.proof_plan: Transport to the fixed law of X_1; domination by |X_1| gives convergence of individual truncated means; apply deterministic Cesaro averaging.

items.support: IID real X_n with E|X_1|<infinity satisfy S_n/n -> E X_1 almost surely.
items.proof_plan: Truncate at index n, preserve mutual independence, apply the variance strong law to bounded Y_n, add the Cesaro means and remove finitely many truncation errors. No ergodic theorem or pairwise random-series convergence is used. Clause audit: use only the almost-sure conclusion. In the convergence-criterion supplier, steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove this without the L2-completeness step 1.2: the variance-tail bound gives P(sup_{j>=m}|S_j-S_m|>t)<=v_m/t^2; the decreasing Cauchy-oscillation events have probability tending to zero. Countably many rational tolerances give a measurable finite path limit; Kronecker then gives the asserted normalization. The unused L2 clause omits its published completeness supplier's countable-choice hypothesis; that clause is Phase-3 debt, not used here.

items.support: If IID real X_n have S_n/n converging almost surely to a finite (possibly initially random) limit, then E|X_1|<infinity and the limit equals E X_1 almost surely.
items.proof_plan: X_n/n=S_n/n-((n-1)/n) S_{n-1}/(n-1)->0. Thus {|X_n|>n} occurs finitely often. The contrapositive of BC2 forces summable common-law tails; the tail lemma gives L1, and the preceding law identifies the limit. Do not assume the initial finite limit is constant.

items.support: Pairwise independent identically distributed integrable real X_n satisfy S_n/n -> E X_1 almost surely.
items.proof_plan: Split into positive and negative parts. For each alpha=1+1/r, use def-integer-power and lem-integer-part to set k_j=floor(alpha^j). For all sufficiently large j, k_j>=alpha^j/2; hence, by nonnegative summation, the coefficient of Var(Y_m) in sum_j Var(T_{k_j})/k_j^2 is at most 4 sum_{j:alpha^j>=m}alpha^(-2j)<=C_alpha m^-2, where thm-geometric-series evaluates the geometric tail (the finitely many initial j are absorbed in C_alpha). Thus the variance series is finite. Pairwise independence suffices for variance addition. Chebyshev and BC1 give subsequence convergence. Monotonicity of nonnegative T_n bounds liminf and limsup by mu/alpha and alpha mu. Intersect the countably many full-measure events and let r increase. The design cubic subsequence is not justified by this L1 estimate; geometric subsequences are the verified correction.

items.support: On the countable product carrying IID integrable real coordinates, the left shift is measure preserving and ergodic, and Birkhoff recovers S_n/n -> E X_1 almost surely. Assume AC for the countable-product construction and ergodic supplier.
items.proof_plan: Assume AC for the published countable-product construction (covering its CC and DC hypotheses). On the canonical countable product of the common real law, the left shift is measurable because the pullback of each coordinate cylinder is the shifted cylinder. Cylinder probabilities are unchanged, since every finite joint law is the same product of the common law; the generating-pi-system theorem then proves measure preservation on the whole product sigma-algebra. For a strictly invariant measurable event E, E=T^-n E for every n. The inverse image T^-n E is measurable with respect to coordinates n,n+1,..., since this holds for cylinders and the class of events whose inverse image is tail-coordinate-measurable is a sigma-algebra. Thus E is a tail event. Kolmogorov zero-one gives P(E) in {0,1}, which is exactly the local definition of ergodicity; no mod-null representative is needed for this definition. Apply the independently proved local ergodic probability theorem to the first coordinate to obtain almost-sure and L1 convergence of its averages to the common mean. This is the Birkhoff route required by the design, not an appeal to the independent IID strong law. The general nonergodic/sigma-finite MT-23 theorem and its remaining programme stay in the future plan and are not consumed here. Local choice bridge: restriction of AC to the prescribed countable family gives def-countable-choice. For any serial relation R on a nonempty set A and prescribed a0, AC selects s(a) in {b:a R b} simultaneously for every a∈A. The earlier thm-recursion constructs a_{n+1}=s(a_n) from a0, proving precisely def-dependent-choice. Thus the independent-copy supplier's CC and DC assumptions hold; no later weak-choice theorem is cited.

items.support: For IID real X_n of finite variance and mean mu, for every epsilon>0, (S_n-n mu)/(sqrt(n)(log n)^(1/2+epsilon))->0 almost surely, n>=2.
items.proof_plan: Use only the general almost-sure conclusion of thm-kolmogorov-strong-law-under-summable-normalized-variances, not its published logarithmic-rate clause. Set b_1=b_2=1 and b_n=sqrt(n)(log n)^(1/2+epsilon) for n>=3. The logarithm order law and positive-real-power laws, with the derivative formula, make b_n positive, nondecreasing, and divergent. For 2^k<=n<2^(k+1), def-integer-power and the logarithm order law give 1/[n(log n)^(1+2epsilon)] <= 1/[n(k log 2)^(1+2epsilon)], so the whole block is at most (log 2)^(-1-2epsilon) k^(-1-2epsilon). The p-series theorem and direct comparison make the variance-normalizer series finite. IID variance is constant, so the general conclusion gives the stated rate. This local dyadic argument does not use the defective published rate proof or its L2 clause.

items.support: Assume AC for the product-space construction. On {0,1} with P({1})=p and P({0})=1-p, independent product coordinates X_n satisfy S_n/n -> p almost surely, including p=0,1.
items.proof_plan: The displayed two-atom law is a probability measure. Its finite expectation sums give E X_1=p and E X_1^2=p, hence Var(X_1)=p(1-p), including p=0,1. Apply the independent-copy supplier and then the finite-variance law. Local choice bridge: restriction of AC to the prescribed countable family gives def-countable-choice. For any serial relation R on a nonempty set A and prescribed a0, AC selects s(a) in {b:a R b} simultaneously for every a∈A. The earlier thm-recursion constructs a_{n+1}=s(a_n) from a0, proving precisely def-dependent-choice. Thus the independent-copy supplier's CC and DC assumptions hold; no later weak-choice theorem is cited.

items.support: For IID random elements and a fixed measurable set A, n^-1 sum 1_A(X_k)->P(X_1 in A) almost surely. For a countable specified class, one common full-measure event works.
items.proof_plan: Apply the strong law to bounded indicators and intersect countably many events; no simultaneous claim over every measurable set.

items.support: Assume AC for the product-space construction. Let X have CDF F(x)=0 for x<1 and F(x)=1-x^(-3/2) for x>=1 (equivalently density (3/2)x^(-5/2) on [1,infinity)). IID copies have mean 3 and infinite second moment, but their sample mean converges almost surely to 3.
items.proof_plan: The real-power calculus shows F is nondecreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 and 1, so the probability-law/CDF correspondence realizes it (its derivative on (1,infinity) is the stated density). Its tail is P(X>t)=1 for 0<=t<1 and t^(-3/2) for t>=1. Layer cake gives E X=1+integral_1^infinity t^(-3/2)dt=3, while the L-p layer-cake formula gives E X^2=1+2 integral_1^infinity t^(-1/2)dt=infinity, using the real-power antiderivatives. AC supplies the countable product (and its CC use); apply the IID L1 law, not a variance result. Integral-interface closure: each displayed density and moment integrand is continuous on every compact subinterval of its support. Continuous integrability and the second FTC evaluate its proper Riemann integrals; the bounded Riemann/Lebesgue agreement theorem (under the already assumed AC, hence countable choice) identifies those with Lebesgue integrals. Increasing compact truncations and MCT give the full nonnegative integrals, including divergent moments. The indefinite-integral theorem first makes the density integral a measure. The computed interval increments and total mass one identify it with the CDF law by finite-measure pi-system uniqueness; differentiability of a CDF alone is not used as a density theorem. In particular on [1,R], integrate (3/2)t^(-5/2), t^(-3/2), and t^(-1/2) using primitives -t^(-3/2), -2t^(-1/2), and 2t^(1/2). The singleton endpoint has Lebesgue measure zero, and the interval identities therefore also hold for half-open intervals. Local choice bridge: restriction of AC to the prescribed countable family gives def-countable-choice. For any serial relation R on a nonempty set A and prescribed a0, AC selects s(a) in {b:a R b} simultaneously for every a∈A. The earlier thm-recursion constructs a_{n+1}=s(a_n) from a0, proving precisely def-dependent-choice. Thus the independent-copy supplier's CC and DC assumptions hold; no later weak-choice theorem is cited.

items.support: Assume AC for the product-space construction. For independent copies eps_n of the two-point law P(eps_n=1)=P(eps_n=-1)=1/2 and X_n=n^(1/4) eps_n, S_n/n->0 almost surely although Var(X_n)=sqrt(n) is unbounded.
items.proof_plan: The displayed two-point law is a probability measure, and its finite sums give E eps_n=0, E eps_n^2=1, and Var(eps_n)=1. The real-power laws then give E X_n=0 and Var(X_n)=n^(1/2), so Var(X_n)/n^2=n^(-3/2); the real p-series theorem proves summability. Use only the general almost-sure conclusion of the normalized-variance supplier. AC supplies the independent copies; its unused L2 clause is not used here. Local choice bridge: restriction of AC to the prescribed countable family gives def-countable-choice. For any serial relation R on a nonempty set A and prescribed a0, AC selects s(a) in {b:a R b} simultaneously for every a∈A. The earlier thm-recursion constructs a_{n+1}=s(a_n) from a0, proving precisely def-dependent-choice. Thus the independent-copy supplier's CC and DC assumptions hold; no later weak-choice theorem is cited.

items.support: Assume AC for the product-space construction. There are integrable real X_n with S_n/n->0 in probability but (S_n-E S_n)/n not tending to zero almost surely.
items.proof_plan: On ((0,1),B,Lebesgue), let U(u)=u; thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind gives P(U<=t)=t for 0<t<1. Construct IID copies U_n using the independent-copy supplier and set B_n=1_{U_n<=1/(n+1)}. Measurable coordinate transformations preserve independence. Let B_0=0 and X_n=n B_n-(n-1)B_{n-1}. Then S_n/n=B_n and E S_n/n=1/(n+1)->0. BC2 gives B_n=1 infinitely often and also B_n=0 infinitely often. Thus no almost-sure convergence. The summands X_n need not be independent; the rare events are independent. The bare B_n sequence alone would only refute a convergence-mode implication, not a sample-mean law. Local choice bridge: restriction of AC to the prescribed countable family gives def-countable-choice. For any serial relation R on a nonempty set A and prescribed a0, AC selects s(a) in {b:a R b} simultaneously for every a∈A. The earlier thm-recursion constructs a_{n+1}=s(a_n) from a0, proving precisely def-dependent-choice. Thus the independent-copy supplier's CC and DC assumptions hold; no later weak-choice theorem is cited.

items.support: Assume AC for the product-space construction. IID standard Cauchy variables cannot have sample means converging almost surely to any finite random limit. Their sample means are standard Cauchy for each n and hence cannot converge in probability to a finite constant.
items.proof_plan: The inverse-tangent calculus makes F(x)=1/2+atan(x)/pi a CDF; the probability-law/CDF correspondence realizes the standard Cauchy law with density f_1(x)=1/[pi(1+x^2)]. The logarithm primitive gives integral |x|f_1(x)dx=infinity, so the necessity theorem rules out any finite almost-sure sample-mean limit. For scale densities f_a, the product joint-law theorem, Tonelli, and improper-integral substitution reduce the sum law to f_a*f_b. With q=x^2+b^2-a^2 and H=q^2+4a^2x^2=(x^2+(a+b)^2)(x^2+(a-b)^2), partial fractions give, for H>0, 1/[(y^2+a^2)((y-x)^2+b^2)]=(Ay+B)/(y^2+a^2)+[-A(y-x)+D]/((y-x)^2+b^2), A=2x/H, B=q/H, D=(x^2+a^2-b^2)/H. On [-R,R], the logarithmic terms have joint limit zero and the inverse-tangent terms give pi(B/a+D/b)=pi(a+b)/(ab(x^2+(a+b)^2)). The only H=0 case is x=0,a=b; this singleton is Lebesgue-null and is not needed for the a.e. density identity. Thus f_a*f_b=f_(a+b) almost everywhere. Induction and scaling make every sample mean standard Cauchy, whose every finite-center neighborhood has probability below one, so it cannot converge in probability to a finite constant. AC supplies the product construction and its CC use. Integral-interface closure: each displayed density and moment integrand is continuous on every compact subinterval of its support. Continuous integrability and the second FTC evaluate its proper Riemann integrals; the bounded Riemann/Lebesgue agreement theorem (under the already assumed AC, hence countable choice) identifies those with Lebesgue integrals. Increasing compact truncations and MCT give the full nonnegative integrals, including divergent moments. The indefinite-integral theorem first makes the density integral a measure. The computed interval increments and total mass one identify it with the CDF law by finite-measure pi-system uniqueness; differentiability of a CDF alone is not used as a density theorem. For each a>0, the primitive of f_a is atan(x/a)/pi; its limits give total mass one. For the moment on [0,R], the primitive of x/(pi(1+x^2)) is log(1+x^2)/(2pi), tending to infinity. Apply the compact integral-agreement bridge to the rational convolution integrand before taking R to infinity; cancellation of logarithmic terms is done on the finite interval, never by subtracting infinite integrals. To justify the sum-density interface without assuming a change-of-variables theorem for arbitrary measurable functions, first test a finite interval (u,v]: the product law and Tonelli give integral f_a(y) integral_(u-y)^(v-y) f_b(z) dz dy. For each fixed y, the compact continuous-integral substitution z=x-y, justified by FTC, changes the inner integral to integral_u^v f_b(x-y) dx. Tonelli then gives the convolution density on that interval; finite-measure pi-system uniqueness extends equality to all Borel sets. The positive scaling of a Cauchy law is likewise verified on intervals by its inverse-tangent CDF and then by uniqueness. Local choice bridge: restriction of AC to the prescribed countable family gives def-countable-choice. For any serial relation R on a nonempty set A and prescribed a0, AC selects s(a) in {b:a R b} simultaneously for every a∈A. The earlier thm-recursion constructs a_{n+1}=s(a_n) from a0, proving precisely def-dependent-choice. Thus the independent-copy supplier's CC and DC assumptions hold; no later weak-choice theorem is cited.

items.support: On {0,1} with P({0})=P({1})=1/2, let X be the identity and X_n=X for every n. Then S_n/n=X never converges almost surely to its mean 1/2.
items.proof_plan: The displayed two-atom assignment is a probability measure and its finite expectation sum gives E X=1/2. Since every X_n=X, S_n/n=X, whose deviation from 1/2 has absolute value 1/2 on both atoms. Marginals are identical but coordinates are dependent.

items.support: Let T preserve a probability measure P and let f be an integrable real-valued measurable function. Write S_k f=sum_{j=0}^{k-1} f composed with T^j, M_N=max(0,S_1 f,...,S_N f), and E_N={M_N>0}. Then integral_{E_N} f dP>=0. The same inequality holds on E={sup_{k>=1} S_k f>0}.
items.proof_plan: For each k<=N, S_k f=f+(S_{k-1} f) composed with T, with S_0=0. Thus f+M_N composed with T>=S_k f. On E_N this gives f>=M_N-M_N composed with T. Outside E_N, M_N=0 and M_N composed with T>=0, hence pointwise f 1_{E_N}>=M_N-M_N composed with T on the whole space. All expressions are measurable and integrable: 0<=M_N<=sum_{j<N}|f| composed with T^j, and integral invariance bounds its integral by N integral|f|. Integrate the pointwise inequality; invariance cancels the two M_N integrals. Since E_N increases to E and |f 1_{E_N}|<=|f|, dominated convergence gives the infinite-horizon inequality. No recurrence theorem, conditional expectation, Hilbert-space theorem or independence argument is used.

items.support: If T is an ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a probability space and f is an integrable real-valued measurable function, then A_n f=n^-1 sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f composed with T^j converges almost surely and in L1 to the constant integral f dP. No invertibility assumption is required.
items.proof_plan: Put c=integral f and h=f-c. The measurable extended-real L=limsup_n A_n h is exactly T-invariant: A_n h(Tx)=((n+1)/n) A_{n+1}h(x)-h(x)/n. Removing a finite initial term, multiplying by positive scalars tending to one, and subtracting a sequence tending to zero preserve extended-real limsup; this follows by comparing eventual upper bounds and subsequences approaching the limsup, with the same comparisons at either infinity. Therefore D={L>epsilon} is strictly invariant for each epsilon>0. Set g=(h-epsilon)1_D. Invariance gives S_n g=1_D(S_n h-n epsilon), so {sup_n S_n g>0}=D: outside D all sums vanish, while inside D the defining strict limsup inequality supplies a positive sum. The preceding maximal lemma gives integral_D(h-epsilon)>=0. Ergodicity makes P(D) either zero or one. If it were one, that integral would be integral h-epsilon=-epsilon, a contradiction. Hence P(D)=0. Apply this for epsilon=1/m and for -h, and use countable subadditivity to obtain limsup A_n h<=0<=liminf A_n h almost surely. For L1 convergence let f_K=f 1_{|f|<=K}. Its averages converge almost surely to c_K=integral f_K by the result just proved and are bounded by K, so dominated convergence gives integral|A_n f_K-c_K|->0. Integral invariance and the triangle inequality yield integral|A_n f-c|<=2 integral|f-f_K|+integral|A_n f_K-c_K|. The first term tends to zero with K by dominated convergence, uniformly in n; then let n tend to infinity. This proves both conclusions using the local maximal lemma, not the IID strong law, so the agreement corollary is not circular. The function in the hypothesis is finite-valued; no subtraction of infinite values or choice of a representative is hidden.

contents.name: Local normalization of Durrett Example1.6.11 density from published Gaussian integral
contents.support: Use exp positivity and differentiability to obtain a positive continuous Borel function. On [-n,n], ordinary one-variable substitution t=x/sqrt(2), with constant derivative 1/sqrt(2), gives integral exp(-x^2/2) dx = sqrt(2) integral from -n/sqrt(2) to n/sqrt(2) exp(-t^2) dt. The compact Riemann/Lebesgue comparison applies because the functions are continuous, bounded and Riemann integrable; AC supplies its explicitly required countable choice by applying AC directly to the countably indexed family of nonempty sets; repeated sets reuse their selected member. Monotone convergence of the nonnegative truncations to R gives the Lebesgue integral as the limit of those compact integrals. The earlier Gaussian integral, proved as an improper Riemann integral, makes the limit sqrt(2)*sqrt(pi)=sqrt(2*pi); square-root uniqueness proves the last equality. Homogeneity gives mass one. This uses no later multidimensional Borel/Radon bridge, characteristic function, or normal-law theorem.

contents.name: Example1.6.11 standard normal and affine normal-law convention
contents.support: The preceding positive Borel density induces a measure by the published indefinite-integral theorem, and its computed total mass is one. Every affine map is continuous by the epsilon-delta estimate |(m+sigma*x)-(m+sigma*y)|=sigma*|x-y| (constant case separate), hence Borel measurable. Its pushforward is a probability measure by the published law lemma. When sigma=0 its inverse image of E is all R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, exactly delta_m. These definitions precede every Gaussian example; no characteristic-function theorem, variance computation or unproved multivariate construction is consumed.

items.support: Let S be Polish, equipped with its Borel sigma-algebra. A Borel probability law is a countably additive probability measure on that sigma-algebra. Choose a compatible complete metric when a construction needs it.
items.proof_plan: Reuse the topological definition of Polish. An empty space carries no probability law.

items.support: For Borel probability measures on a metric space, mu_n=>mu means integral f dmu_n -> integral f dmu for every bounded continuous real f.
items.proof_plan: Bounded Borel functions are integrable for probability measures. The definition also applies beyond Polish spaces.

items.support: Measurable random elements X_n and X with a common metric state space converge in distribution when their laws converge weakly; their underlying probability spaces need not agree.
items.proof_plan: Use pushforward laws, without choosing a coupling.

items.support: For metric-space Borel probabilities, weak convergence is equivalent to convergence of integrals of bounded uniformly continuous functions, the closed-set limsup inequality, the open-set liminf inequality, and convergence on all Borel mu-continuity sets. No completeness is required.
items.proof_plan: Use f_m=(1-m d(x,F))_+ for nonempty closed F, handle F=empty separately, then complements and interior/closure sandwich. For continuity sets=>tests, partition the bounded range of f into intervals whose endpoints have zero f_*mu mass, bound f by finite simple functions with uniform error. Finitely many endpoints suffice; countably many atoms are excluded by finite measure. No compactness or Skorokhod used.

items.support: For real random variables, the earlier CDF continuity-point definition of convergence in distribution agrees with weak convergence of laws.
items.proof_plan: Weak convergence gives convergence on (-infinity,t] at nonatoms. Conversely partition a bounded interval at continuity points, control both tails using CDFs there, and approximate each bounded continuous test uniformly on that interval.

items.support: Bounded continuous real functions determine Borel probabilities on a metric space; a weakly convergent sequence has at most one limit.
items.proof_plan: Equal test integrals give equal closed-set masses by distance approximations; closed sets form a pi-system generating Borel sets. Use finite-measure uniqueness.

items.support: For metric spaces S,T, measurable g:S->T, mu_n=>mu and mu(D_g)=0 imply g_*mu_n=>g_*mu. In particular X_n=>X implies g(X_n)=>g(X). Assume D_g Borel, as holds for metric-valued maps by the oscillation criterion.
items.proof_plan: For closed F in T, closure(g^-1 F) is contained in g^-1 F union D_g. Apply the closed-set bound. Prove D_g is Borel via local oscillation: continuity set is intersection over r of the open set of points having a neighborhood with image diameter<1/r.

items.support: For S-valued random elements X_n,Y_n on a common probability space (or one space per n), with S metric, P(d(X_n,Y_n)>epsilon)->0 for every epsilon>0 and X_n=>X, one has Y_n=>X. Require measurability of the distances, automatic for separable metric S.
items.proof_plan: For closed F, P(Y_n in F)<=P(X_n in {d(x,F)<=epsilon})+P(d(X_n,Y_n)>epsilon). Apply portmanteau to the closed enlargement and decrease epsilon to zero. No unproved product weak convergence needed.

items.support: A family A of Borel probability measures on S is tight if for every epsilon>0 some compact K satisfies sup_{mu in A}mu(S\K)<epsilon. The empty family is vacuously tight.
items.proof_plan: Use one compact set for the entire family.

items.proof_plan: Distinguish relative sequential compactness from compactness of the family itself.

items.support: Assuming AC, every Borel probability on a Polish space is tight.
items.proof_plan: Apply the published inner-regularity theorem to the whole space. Also display its complete-metric finite-net proof: intersect finite unions of closed balls with summable probability losses, then completeness plus total boundedness. Propagate its countable-choice hypothesis via the authorized AC assumption.

items.support: Assuming AC, C(K,R) is separable in supremum norm for every compact metric K. In particular a countable class determines all integrals of continuous functions uniformly.
items.proof_plan: Choose finite 1/m-nets. With a fixed countable dense union D, use finite minima of rational constants plus integer multiples of d(x,a), clipped at rational bounds. Uniform continuity on K allows Lipschitz inf-envelope approximation of any continuous f, then approximate finitely many coefficients and centers. Prove both approximation inequalities explicitly; constant functions cover a singleton and K=empty separately. Detailed estimate: given |f|<=M and tolerance eta, choose delta for oscillation<eta and an integer L with L delta>2M. Then g(x)=inf_y[f(y)+L d(x,y)] satisfies f(x)-eta<=g(x)<=f(x). Replace the infimum by a minimum over a sufficiently fine finite net and replace each f(a) by a rational within eta. The net error is <=eta+L times its mesh, uniformly in x; make both small. Clip at rational bounds containing f(K). The countable collection of all such finite rational formulas on the fixed D is dense.

references.title: van Gaans, Proposition 5.3 and §6; diagonal replacement for compact-case functional argument

items.support: Assuming AC, every sequence of Borel probabilities on a compact metric K has a weakly convergent subsequence.
items.proof_plan: Diagonalize bounded integrals on the countable dense tests. Uniform approximation extends the limits to a positive linear functional L on C(K) with L(1)=1. Apply the published positive RMK representation on compact Hausdorff K, where C_c(K)=C(K), to obtain a probability measure. This avoids using Banach-Alaoglu or confusing compactness with sequential compactness. RMK uniqueness is not needed: any representing probability measure is an adequate subsequential limit.

references.title: van Gaans, Theorem 5.2, Proposition 5.3, Lemma 5.4, pp. 14–18

items.support: Assuming AC, a family of Borel probability measures on a Polish space is tight iff it is relatively sequentially compact for weak convergence.
items.proof_plan: Forward: embed S homeomorphically into the Hilbert cube H, extract a subsequence of pushed laws by the compact-law lemma, and take compact K_m in S with uniform loss<1/m. Portmanteau gives limit mass one on E=union_m image(K_m), a Borel subset of image(S). Define mu(B)=nu(E intersect image(B)); image(B) is Borel relative to image(S), hence E intersect image(B) is Borel in H. For closed F in S, choose closed Z in H with Z intersect image(S)=image(F); then mu_n(F)=nu_n(Z), and nu(Z)=mu(F). Portmanteau proves convergence. Reverse: for any countable open cover U_i and epsilon>0, failure of a uniform finite initial cover gives mu_n(union_{i<=n} U_i)<=1-epsilon. Extract a weak limit and use open bounds for each fixed initial union, contradicting continuity from below. Apply this uniform-cover fact to dense balls at each scale, take finite CLOSED ball unions and intersect; summable losses and complete total boundedness yield a common compact K. AC supplies selections; no local compactness of S is assumed. For the Hilbert cube, the published weighted countable-product metric is complete; finite rational meshes on finitely many coordinates and a small geometric tail prove total boundedness. Thus the compact-law lemma applies without invoking an undeclared Tychonoff theorem.

items.support: Assuming AC, {mu,mu_1,mu_2,...} is tight whenever mu_n=>mu on a Polish space.
items.proof_plan: Any sequence selected from this set has a constant subsequence or a subsequence whose indices tend to infinity, and thus a weak limit. Apply Prokhorov.

items.support: Assuming AC, every tight sequence of Polish-space Borel probability laws has a subsequence converging weakly to a probability law on that same space.
items.proof_plan: Use the forward implication; mass stays one.

items.support: For probabilities mu,nu on a metric space, pi(mu,nu) is the infimum of epsilon>0 such that both mu(F)<=nu(F^[epsilon])+epsilon and nu(F)<=mu(F^[epsilon])+epsilon for every closed F, with F^[epsilon]={x:d(x,F)<=epsilon} and empty enlargement empty.
items.proof_plan: The admissible set contains every epsilon>=1, and is bounded below by zero. Fix CLOSED enlargements and closed test sets as in the design; the metric lemma proves equivalence to the standard open-enlargement Borel-set convention by arbitrarily small epsilon slack.

items.support: The closed-set closed-enlargement definition is a metric, bounded above by 1, on Borel probabilities of a metric space; it equals the infimum in the all-Borel open-enlargement convention.
items.proof_plan: Symmetry and self-distance are immediate. For triangle use (F^[a])^[b] subset F^[a+b], with all these sets closed. Infimum zero gives agreement on every closed F by continuity from above, then Borel uniqueness. For equivalence, B subset closure(B) and closure(B)^[a] subset B^(a+delta); conversely closed enlargement contains open enlargement. Let delta decrease to zero. This uses no compact-inner regularity in non-Polish spaces.

items.support: Assuming AC, for a separable metric S and Borel probability mu there are countable refining Borel partitions P_k with every nonempty atom of diameter<=2^-k and mu-null boundary. They generate Borel(S).
items.proof_plan: Choose a countable dense set. For each center and scale choose a radius in a fixed interval avoiding the countably many radii with positive-measure spheres; the balls cover S. Disjointize by subtracting earlier balls and refine finitely many levels. Each atom boundary lies in a finite union of selected sphere boundaries; each level countable. Any open set is the union of the atoms whose diameter is small enough and that contain its points. Empty atoms are discarded. AC covers all countable choices of radii and atom representatives.

references.title: van Gaans, Theorem 4.2 and Lemma 4.3, pp. 10–12

items.support: Assuming AC, on a separable metric space pi(mu_n,mu)->0 iff mu_n=>mu; completeness is not required.
items.proof_plan: Metric convergence gives closed-set bounds via shrinking enlargements. Conversely take finitely many small boundary-null balls covering mu-mass>1-delta. Their finitely many unions have converging masses; for any Borel B take the union of the selected balls meeting B. It lies in B^epsilon and covers B except for the small-mass complement. Both inequalities follow with total error<=3delta, delta<epsilon/3. Use slack to match closed-neighborhood convention.

items.support: Assuming AC, on a nonempty complete separable metric S, a sequence of countable refining partitions of vanishing atom diameters yields, for each Borel probability sigma, a measurable map T_sigma:(0,1)->S with law sigma by nested interval allocation.
items.proof_plan: Allocate half-open intervals of lengths sigma(A) inside each parent interval in a fixed child ordering, discarding the countable set of all endpoints. Select a representative x_A from each nonempty atom. For any remaining u, selected atoms are nested and representatives are Cauchy, so completeness yields T_sigma(u); use a fixed base point on the endpoint set. Measurability follows as a pointwise limit of countably valued measurable maps: preimages of closed F are expressed using d(x_A,F) and countable operations. For each bounded Lipschitz f, the integral of the representative map equals sum sigma(A)f(x_A) and differs from integral f dsigma by at most Lip(f)2^-k. DCT identifies the law of T_sigma with sigma; distance test functions determine closed-set masses. Do NOT assert that nested half-open atoms intersect or that the limit belongs to its atom. Work on ((0,1), B((0,1)), Lebesgue): the box theorem gives each allocated interval its prescribed length and total mass one; the countable-null-set proposition removes all endpoints. The assumed AC supplies CC by restricting a choice function to the given countably indexed family. Endpoint sets and intervals are Borel; their nullity therefore holds for the Borel restriction without completing the probability space.

references.title: Advanced Probability, Theorem 5.29, pp. 65–67, repaired as in the preceding lemma

items.support: Assuming AC, if mu_n=>mu on a Polish space, then there are random elements Y_n,Y on ((0,1),B,Lebesgue) with these laws and Y_n->Y almost surely.
items.proof_plan: Choose partitions with mu-null boundaries and a compatible complete metric. Realize all laws with identical atom order and representatives. Every fixed atom mass converges; each of its interval endpoints is a finite sum within its parent plus the parent endpoint, so endpoints converge inductively down any fixed finite address. For u outside the countable collection of limit endpoints, every fixed-level chosen atom for mu_n eventually equals the mu atom. The two representative limits lie in that atom's closure, giving distance<=2^-k. Intersect the exceptional null sets for countably many laws and levels. Completeness is essential to construct the limits.

items.support: For each finite d>=1 there is a countable uniformly dense subset of C_c(R^d) in its supremum norm, including compact cutoff functions increasing to 1. Convergence of probability integrals on this class to a probability mu implies weak convergence to mu.
items.proof_plan: Use compactly supported piecewise multilinear functions on rational rectangular grids with rational vertex values that are zero at every boundary vertex of an integer cube, and extend them by zero. Face interpolation then makes the extension continuous. Given f in C_c, choose a cube whose boundary misses supp(f); uniform continuity, a finite rational grid, and rational approximation of the zero boundary values give uniform density. Include rational piecewise-multilinear cutoffs chi_m equal to one on [-m,m]^d and zero outside [-m-1,m+1]^d. Test convergence for a cutoff of mu-integral near one bounds the mass outside its support uniformly for late n. Approximate a bounded continuous test times a larger cutoff in C_c; the remaining integrals are bounded by the small tails. No assertion that C_b(R^d) is norm separable. Uniform continuity on the selected Euclidean cube follows directly from compactness by a finite ball cover; the grid and rational approximants are chosen finitely for each tolerance, so no arbitrary selection principle is used. The nonnegative cutoffs increase pointwise to 1, so integral monotone convergence gives integral chi_m dmu increasing to 1; convergence of a bounded numerical sequence alone would not identify that limit.

items.support: Assume AC. The uniform probability on {1/n,2/n,...,1} converges weakly to uniform measure on [0,1].
items.proof_plan: AC supplies countable choice by restricting its selection function to a countably indexed family; this is the inherited assumption used by Heine-Cantor and the Lebesgue-box theorem. Let lambda be Lebesgue measure restricted to [0,1], of total mass one. The grid law assigns each k/n mass 1/n; countable additivity follows by summing the membership indicators of its finitely many atoms. For bounded continuous real f, put s_n(x)=f(k/n) on ((k-1)/n,k/n] and s_n(0)=f(0). The singleton {0} is null and each interval has mass 1/n, so the simple integral gives integral s_n dlambda = n^-1 sum f(k/n) = integral f dmu_n. Uniform continuity makes |s_n-f| uniformly less than any prescribed epsilon for sufficiently large n. Linearity, the real integral triangle inequality and monotonicity bound the absolute integral difference by epsilon times lambda([0,1])=epsilon. This proves weak convergence directly, without a Riemann/Lebesgue identification theorem. No arbitrary choice is used by the finite grid calculation itself.

items.support: For probability laws on R^d, sup_mu integral ||x||^p dmu<=C with p>0 implies tightness.
items.proof_plan: lem-metrics-on-rn identifies ||x|| as the Euclidean distance to zero. For R>0, the real-power laws identify {|x|>R} with {||x||^p>R^p}; Markov gives mass at most C/R^p. Closed Euclidean balls are compact by Heine--Borel, so choosing R with C/R^p<epsilon proves tightness.

items.support: Assume AC. If m_n->m and sigma_n>=0 tends to sigma>=0, then N(m_n,sigma_n^2)=>N(m,sigma^2), with N(m,0)=delta_m.
items.proof_plan: On the explicitly constructed standard-normal probability space let Z(x)=x. The affine variables m_n+sigma_n*Z tend pointwise to m+sigma*Z, including sigma=0. Continuous bounded test functions therefore converge pointwise and have one integrable constant bound; DCT and the published change-of-variables-for-expectation identity prove weak convergence of their laws. No characteristic-function or future supplier.

items.support: Assume AC. If real laws mu_n=>mu have CDFs F_n,F, then on ((0,1),B,Lebesgue), U(u)=u and Q_n(U)->Q(U) almost surely with the prescribed laws, where Q(u)=inf{x:F(x)>=u}.
items.proof_plan: thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind makes U(u)=u uniform on the displayed Lebesgue interval. At each continuity point u of Q, choose continuity points a<Q(u)<b so F(a)<u<F(b), making Q_n(u) lie in (a,b] eventually. If Q(u) equals an endpoint, choose a,b on either side using continuity of Q at u. FRODA makes the discontinuity set of Q countable, and prop-countable-subsets-of-rn makes it Lebesgue-null; omit u=0,1. Generalized-inverse measurability and its CDF are checked. AC declares the countable-choice use in the cited correspondence/FRODA machinery.
